We simulated here a simple neural network model consisting of a CA3 neuronal layer (nCA3 = 200 cells in CA3) projecting to a CA1 neuronal layer (see schematic in Fig. 3d). Learning was performed for nCA1 = 500 cells in CA1 (which also means 500 repeats of the simulation; each simulation was performed for one independent target spatial map in the CA1 output layer); the firing-properties of the target CA1 maps were matched to the empirical statistics of our CA1 maps in the long tunnel (Methods). a, Node perturbation learning rule. Left, map reconstruction errors for the output CA1 maps, as a function of the learning time (the learning-time [steps] is the number of simulation-epochs normalized by the number of spatial map bins). The reconstruction error was averaged over 250 randomly selected CA1 maps out of the total of 500, for each learning step, until the error reached a target error (dashed horizontal lines show three different options for the target error). Number of fields in the CA3 input spatial maps (between 1–6 fields) is indicated by different line colours. Note the shorter learning-time for sparse maps in CA3 input neurons (with 1–2 fields) vs. dense maps in CA3 input neurons (with 5–6 fields). Middle, average learning time as a function of the number of fields in the CA3 input spatial maps (the three curves are plots for the three target-errors shown on the left). The upper-most curve is the same as plotted in Fig. 3e, here plotted in logarithmic y-scale. Right, distribution of the absolute value of the synaptic weights connecting CA3 to CA1 after learning (n = 105 synapses). Note that the distribution of the synaptic weights for the case of single-field CA3 input has a heavier tail, compared to multiple-fields CA3 input. In our simulations, an intuitive explanation for the emergence of heavy-tailed distribution of synaptic weights only for the case of single-field maps in CA3 is that in this case there is a high likelihood that each field of the output CA1 map arises from one strong CA3 → CA1 connection. In this scenario, the synaptic weight distribution is heavy-tailed, i.e. it has a large fraction of strong connections. It remains to be tested whether such heavy tailed distribution of synaptic weights indeed exists in the biological case of real CA3 → CA1 synapses. We note that such heavy-tailed distribution of synaptic weights is consistent with experimental measurements of synaptic weight distributions in multiple brain areas88,89,90. b, Weight perturbation learning rule, plotted as in a. This alternative learning-rule (Methods) also produced results of faster learning for sparse CA3 input neurons, consistent with the node perturbation learning rule. c, Simulation of learning with additional inputs from CA2/entorhinal cortex (EC). During learning (using the node perturbation rule), synaptic weights between CA3 and CA1 were adjusted (learned) while CA1 cells received additional Gaussian-distributed inputs that were not learned, accounting for non-CA3 inputs to the CA1 layer, such as those from EC and CA2. This additional component had a variance matched to that of the learned component of the map (Methods). Despite the presence of these additional external inputs, learning remained faster for sparse CA3 input neurons (1–2 fields in CA3). Plotted as in a. Note that error values are higher than in a-b (due to the additional inputs), and the target error was adjusted accordingly. d, Simulation of learning after a small perturbation to an already-learned CA1 map (using the node perturbation learning rule). After the network reached the small target reconstruction error, i.e. converged close to the desired CA1 output and exhibited stable synaptic weights, a local perturbation was introduced in the CA1 target maps, initiating the learning process again. The perturbation was localized, limited to an 8-m area in the output maps. Left, the reconstruction error as a function of the learning time, plotted as in a. Inset, zoom-in on early learning steps, showing that the error is lower for the case of single-field input from CA3 (cyan) already after the first learning step (note that learning steps do not have discrete values, because we plot the learning steps per spatial bin). Middle, the average learning time as a function of the number of fields in the CA3 input spatial maps, plotted again similarly to Fig. 3f (independent simulation). Right, distribution of the absolute value of the synaptic weights, plotted as in a. e, Simulations of learning of two context-dependent spatial maps. In these simulations each neuron in CA3 had two different sets of maps, corresponding to two different contexts, which serve as input into CA1 neurons. Each CA1 neuron was required to produce two distinct output target maps, one for each context, using a single set of synaptic weights linking input and output maps. The synaptic weights were updated according to the node-perturbation learning rule, with training protocol that alternated between the two contexts. Left, the reconstruction error as a function of the learning steps per spatial bin for the two maps. Middle, learning time as a function of the number of fields in CA3 maps (same as Extended Data Fig. 13g). Right, distribution of the absolute value of the synaptic weights. Plotted as in a. Overall, these results show that the learning of new or modified spatial maps is substantially faster for a sparse single-field input from CA3 as compared to a multiple-fields input from CA3.

This analysis is based on a single bat (bat no. 1) with simultaneous recordings from both CA1 and CA3 during the first exposure to the tunnel (day 1 in the tunnel); thus, the amount of data here is limited — but importantly, this analysis provides further support for the model in Fig. 3d. e, Example of two place cells recorded simultaneously in CA1 (left, grey) and in CA3 (right, purple) during the first exposure of bat no. 1 to the long tunnel – on day 1. Solid lines indicate the population vector correlation over all neurons; shading denotes the 25–75% confidence intervals obtained by randomly subsampling 50% of all cells in day 1 (left) or subsampling 20 cells for both CA1 and CA3 in later days (right; we subsampled 20 cells on day 2 onward to match the number of CA3 cells on day 1); subsampling was done without replacements, 100 repetitions. Note the rapid initial increase in correlation on day 1 for the CA3 population compared with the more gradual rise in CA1 (left panel) – indicating that although spatial fields emerged in both regions within the first 1–3 flights, hippocampal spatial representations stabilized more quickly in CA3 than in CA1 on day 1 (as can be seen in the examples in e). By contrast, the spatial representations were stable in both CA3 and CA1 on day 2 onward, from the first trial, as indicated by the high correlations seen here from the very first trial (right panel). g, Simulations of learning in the network model after a local perturbation to an already-learned map (as in Fig. 3f), demonstrating that changes in CA1 are more localized when input maps in CA3 are sparse. Left panel: by model definition, CA3 shows no change. a, Examples of place cells in CA1 (grey) and CA3 (purple): here we zoomed in on the area of the junction in the tunnel, and plotted examples of place fields near the junction; data plotted for one flight direction (indicated by an arrow at the top). Scale bars, 3 metres in both the x and y axes. Light-grey curves are the flight trajectories for all the flights during the multi-compartment session; dots are spikes (grey dots, CA1; purple dots, CA3; number of flights per cell ranged in these examples between 21–48 flights per-direction). Top row shows four example place cells (cells 45–48), whose place-fields spanned the junction area and fired in both the long compartment and one of the shorter compartments. Bottom row shows three other examples of place cells (cells 49–51), whose place-fields were limited to one of the compartments, and did not span the junction. Cell 52 is an example of a place cell which fired in the junction area both for flights starting from-straight compartment and from-turn compartment. b, Multi-compartment tunnel structure. Below we analysed the neural activity in these 4 compartments: straight 10-m compartment, turn 10-m compartment, long 180-m compartment, and start area: a 10-m area adjacent to the landing ball at the start of the long compartment (the analyses below for the long compartment excluded the start area). c, Place field sizes per compartment for place cells in CA1 (grey, left) and CA3 (purple, right). Each place field was assigned to one of the 4 compartments based on the position of its centre-of-mass (top; weighted average position based on its firing-rate map), or based on the position of its edges (bottom; fields were assigned to a compartment only if they were fully contained inside the compartment; fields that spanned across compartments were discarded). Boxplots of place-field sizes are shown for each compartment; the boxplots denote the median (horizontal line), 25–75% percentiles (box), and 10–90% percentiles (whiskers); the number of place-fields included in each boxplot is indicated below the boxplot. In CA1, when assigning place fields to compartments based on their centre of mass (top), place-fields in the turn compartment were significantly smaller than place-fields in either the straight compartment, long compartment, or start area (Kruskal-Wallis test, with correction for multiple comparisons: * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, ***** P < 10–5). For the second condition (bottom), where place fields were required to be fully contained in each compartment, there was a significant difference in field sizes only between the long compartment and the short compartments – which is expected because this analysis effectively restricted the maximal field size for the small compartment, but not for the long compartment. All the comparisons that are not marked by stars were non-significant. We note that one potential reason for the rather modest differences in the sizes of place-fields between the large and small compartments is that they have similar valence. By contrast, in the natural, real world, non-spatial factors may play an important role in shaping the spatial resolution of the hippocampal place code: For example, a bat cave may be represented at high resolution, with very small place fields, not just because the cave is much smaller than the open environment outside it – but also because the cave entails high valence and sociality. d, Probability of a place-field per spatial bin (the number of firing-rate maps with place fields in that spatial bin divided by all the valid firing-rate maps) along the tunnel, for CA1 (grey) and CA3 (purple). Bin size = 0.2 m, with moving average smoothing of 5 m (boxcar smoothing). Thick lines are for firing-rate maps of to-turn and from-turn flights pooled together, and thin lines are for firing-rate maps of to-straight and from-straight flights pooled together. Vertical thin grey lines indicate the positions of landmarks along the tunnel, and vertical rectangular grey shading indicates the position of the straight and turn compartments. CA3 place cells are sparser, which explains the lower place-field probability seen here in CA3 along the tunnel. We included here only significant place cells × directions, which had at least one place field in at least one of the tunnel compartments (nCA1 = 500 and 583 cells × directions for straight flights and turn flights, respectively; nCA3 = 193 and 159 cells × directions for straight flights and turn flights, respectively). e, Place field density for each compartment (number of fields normalized by compartment length and number of valid firing-rate maps), for CA1 (left) and CA3 (right); note that the bars do not sum up to 1 because the y-axis is density. The field density was modestly higher for the straight and turn compartments relative to the long compartment (two-sided proportions test: * P = 0.04, *** P < 10–3, **** P = 7.2 × 10–5, ***** P < 1.1 × 10–7; all the comparisons that are not marked by stars were non-significant). Overall, we note that the analyses in panels c and e show that there were only slight differences in place-field size and density between the different compartments – which argues against a neuronal compartmentalization of the environment. f, Analysis of differences (Cohen’s d statistic) in the bats’ position in the Y-axis of the tunnel (tunnel’s width) between the two types of forward flights (to-turn vs. to-straight, blue) and between the two types of returning flights (from-turn vs. from-straight, red). Cohen’s d values were similarly low for both forward flights (blue) and return flights (red) between positions 0 m and 150 m in the tunnel, indicating similar Y-positions. Near the junction, Cohen’s d values increased for returning flights, due to the wider turns, but these differences rapidly converged until position 150 m (see also examples of trajectory convergence in panel a). This analysis suggests that Y-axis differences in trajectories are unlikely to underlie the major neuronal differences that we found between the strong retrospective coding and the weak prospective coding (Fig. 5e)—especially between positions 0 m and about 150 m in the tunnel, where we found here no differences in the Y-axis of the trajectories. g-h, No effects of choice availability on the number of place-fields in CA1 and CA3. g, Scatter of the number of fields per firing-rate map in session 1 in the multi-compartment environment, in which the bat had to choose between two landing-balls (Extended Data Fig. 1b-top), versus the number of fields in session 2, in which the bat had no choice (Extended Data Fig. 1b-bottom) – for place cells in CA1 (left, nCA1 = 155 cells) and CA3 (right, nCA3 = 86 cells), from n = 4 bats. Only the forward flight direction (eastward) towards the choice was considered for this analysis. For the y-axis of these scatter-plots (the number of fields in session 1, with-choice), we plotted here the mean between the two options (turn and straight flight); consequently, this mean number of fields could obtain non-integer values that were multiples of 0.5. Dots were jittered for display purposes only. h, Violin plots (distributions) of the number of fields per map in the with-choice situation (session 1) and the no-choice situation (session 2) for place cells in CA1 (left) and CA3 (right). Numbers as in g. Paired two-sided sign-test of the differences between the number of fields under choice vs. no-choice: P = 0.72 and P = 0.17 for CA1 and CA3, respectively (‘NS’, non-significant).

To test if the long-range retrospective coding could be a result of the challenging motor action of the 90° turn at the junction, we did the following: (1) We analysed the echolocation click-rate in the multi-compartment long-tunnel experiments at the Weizmann Institute (panels a-e). (2) We performed additional experiment at Johns Hopkins University to measure the directional aim of Egyptian fruit bat’s sonar clicks as it executed 90° turns and U-turns (180° turns) in a smaller L-shaped environment (panels f-g). (3) We analysed the neuronal responses during flights in the long tunnel at the Weizmann Institute, following U-turns – a motor action that is at least as challenging as 90° turns – in comparison to the neuronal responses following 90° turns (panels h-j). a-e, Analysis of echolocation click-rates in the long tunnel during neural recordings. To exclude the possibility that the observed strong retrospective coding after 90° turns (Fig. 5) is due to an increased rate of echolocation clicks – that is, that the retrospective coding reflects direct sensory or motor responses or changes in attention levels57 – we used U-turns as a control. We found that echolocation click-rates were similar between the two types of turns (90° turns and U-turns), which suggests a similar sensory input and similar attention levels for 90° turns and U-turns – yet the neural representations after the two types of turns were very different (see panels h-j). a-b, Echolocation click-rate recorded from two bats with the largest number of retrospective flights (bats no. 2 and 6), plotted as a function of position along the tunnel, for (a) forward flights to-straight (blue) and to-turn (red), and (b) returning flights from-straight (blue) and from-turn (red). Solid line indicates the median and shading indicates the 10–90% percentiles of echolocation click-rate across n = 42 recording sessions from two bats. Grey rectangle indicates the position of the straight and turn compartments. Note the increased click-rate close to the landing balls at the ends of the tunnel, during landing and take-off, as well as the increased click-rate during the 90° turns (red: note the red peak at the transition into the grey-rectangle zone [i.e., at the junction]). Inset, zoom-in on the junction area. c, Examples of echolocation clicks during U-turns (top), 90° turns (middle) and straight flight passes through the junction (bottom). For each case, five different flight trials are shown (y-axis); these trials show echolocation clicks (vertical ticks) as a function of time relative to the U-turn (top), or relative to the 90° turn (middle), or relative to junction-passing for straight flights (bottom). The 90° turns and straight flights are all for the returning flight direction (after takeoff). All examples were taken from the same bat (bat no. 2), on the same recording day. d, Average echolocation click-rate for 90° turns (red) and U-turns (black) aligned to the time of the turn, and straight flights aligned to junction-passing (blue) (thick line and shaded area: mean ± SEM, with SEM computed over flights; data pooled for two bats with sufficient turning and straight-flying behaviours [bats no. 2 and 6; n = 743 flights with U-turns, n = 895 flights with 90° turns, and n = 795 straight flights across 42 behavioural sessions]); time bin: 100 ms. Note the similar increase in echolocation click-rate during 90° turns and U-turns, suggesting a similar level of attention and arousal – yet the neuronal responses were very different (see panels h-j). e, Retrospective coding score for each CA1 cell as a function of the echolocation click-rate at the turn on the experimental day in which the cell was recorded, for bat no. 2 (purple) and bat no. 6 (green). Retrospective coding scores were calculated as 1–| ρ |, where ρ is the Spearman correlation coefficient between firing-rate maps of the two returning flight types—from-turn vs. from-straight compartment—computed in positions 90–180 metres, where the retrospective coding was most prominent. High retrospective score indicates a low correlation between the two firing-rate maps, i.e. strong retrospective coding. There was no positive correlation between the neuronal retrospective coding score (y-axis) and echolocation click-rate (x-axis) during turning, for any of the two bats (Spearman correlations for these scatter-plots are indicated above the panel). f-g, Echolocation beam aim recording and analysis in a separate group of bats (without neural recordings; n = 12 bats); these control experiments were performed in a small L-shaped tunnel composed of two main chambers connected by a door. A 32-microphone array, arranged in two rows of 16 microphones each, was used to reconstruct the echolocation beam-aim (Methods). f, Three example flight trajectories and echolocation patterns of a bat performing a U-turn (left), a 90° turn (middle), and a straight flight (right) within the L-shaped tunnel. Shown are the bat’s flight trajectories (grey curves) overlayed with the sonar beam axis (sonar beam direction: black, red, and blue lines). g, Boxplots of the sonar-gaze angle deviation relative to the instantaneous flight direction for all the clicks during U-turns (black, n = 298 clicks across 17 trials [flights]), and during 90° turns (red, n = 296 clicks across 16 trials). Boxplots denote the median (horizontal line), 25–75% (box), and 10–90% (whiskers). We considered for this analysis all the clicks within a temporal window of 1 s centred around the maximum curvature of each U-turn or 90° turn. We found no significant difference in sonar-gaze deviation between U-turns and 90° turns (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test: P = 0.49). Straight flights were excluded from the population comparison shown here, because this tunnel’s limited size prevented isolating straight flights without contamination from immediately-preceding turns or immediately-following turns. h-j, Firing-rate maps after U-turns converge rapidly to the typical spatial map. h, Three example cells recorded in CA1 of bat no. 2, showing that there is retrospective coding of past trajectories in flights with 90° turns (compared to straight), but not after U-turns (also compared to straight; we analysed here only U-turns that occurred in the long compartment). For each cell, plotted are only flights in the returning flight direction (see green arrows above the examples). Upper panel, firing-rate maps for each flight type: from-straight (blue), from-turn (red), and after U-turn flights occurring in the long compartment before the junction (black). Lower panels, raster plots of spike positions (x-axis) for different flights (y-axis: time in minutes) for flights from-straight (top, blue), from-turn (middle, red), and after U-turns (bottom, black). Note that in these 3 neurons, the firing-patterns after U-turns (black) resembled strongly the firing-patterns in flights from-straight (blue) rather than flights from-turn (red) – suggesting that the retrospective remapping after 90° turns (as analysed in Fig. 5) is not due to the motor action of turning (which was as prominent in the U-turns as in the 90° turns [or even more prominent]), but rather was likely due to the different past trajectory or context. i, Neuronal population-vector correlations as a function of position along the tunnel, similar to Fig. 5e – correlations computed here for U-turn flights versus flights from-straight (blue), and for U-turn flights versus flights from-turn (red); n = 55 place cells pooled from 9 different days which had at least five U-turns. These population-vector correlation plots show that the spatial tuning in the neuronal population after U-turns was more similar to flights from-straight (blue) than to flights from-turn (red) (note the higher population-vector correlation for the blue line compared to the red line). j, To capture how rapidly the neuronal coding following U-turns converged back to the straight-flight coding, we aligned here the neuronal responses at the single-trial level to the U-turns (we note that U-turns were distributed at various positions along the tunnel). Specifically, we computed the firing-rate maps for individual U-turn flights as a function of distance from the U-turn – with the same bin size and smoothing as regular firing-rate maps (Methods). Shown are correlations between firing-rate maps of individual U-turn flights and mean firing-rate maps of from-straight flights (blue) or from-turn flights (red), plotted as a function of distance after the U-turn (100 cells × directions, n = 447 U-turn flights). Note the correlation is not calculated here between neuronal population-vectors, but between the spatial firing-rate maps of single cells, computed along space using a spatial sliding windows of 20 m. Solid lines, median correlation value across the n = 447 trials (447 U-turn flights); shading, 25–75% percentiles (the variability here is large because it captures firing-rate variability across single trials of U-turns; single-trial data are inherently noisy). Bottom (inset): zoom-in on the 0–10 m immediately after U-turns. Note that after U-turns, the spatial tuning went back to the baseline map very rapidly, within only 2–3 metres (note the rapid increase of the correlation of the U-turn flights with the flights from-straight; see inset: blue). By contrast, the spatial tuning after U-turns was very different from the maps after 90° turns – with very low correlations (inset: red). This implies that the strong remapping (retrospective coding) seen in Fig. 5e-right after 90° turns is not due to the motor act of turning or the associated attention, because we did not observe here such strong remapping after U-turns—even though a U-turn is an even more extreme motor manoeuvre than a 90° turn.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Technology mediation in child sexual exploitation and abuse in Africa and Asia
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Amy Orben
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

As digital access expands rapidly among children worldwide, technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA), including online grooming, sexual solicitation, non-consensual image sharing and sexual extortion, has emerged as urgent yet underexamined category of digital harms1. Despite growing policy attention to online safety, evidence remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where most of the world’s children live2. We analysed nationally representative survey data from 11,912 children aged 12–17 years across 12 countries in eastern and southern Africa and Southeast Asia, collected through the Disrupting Harm project in 2020–2021. We found that one in six internet-using children experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated CSEA, equivalent to over 10 million children. Despite this scale, many experiences went undisclosed, pointing to disclosure as a critical pathway for protection in the digital age. When children did disclose, they relied primarily on informal channels, especially friends, rather than formal reporting mechanisms such as police or helplines. Using Bayesian hierarchical models accounting for cross-country heterogeneity, we find that older children were less likely to disclose, whereas enabling parental mediation of online activities and children’s knowledge of where to seek help after sexual harassment or assault were associated with higher rates of disclosure. These findings provide population-level evidence to inform prevention and response across low- and middle-income countries, where coordinated action by policymakers, law enforcement and technology companies is urgently needed to protect all children.

Content warning: this Article contains information about child sexual exploitation and abuse, which some readers may find upsetting.

Rapid digitization is driving increasing research on the online safety of children worldwide1, yet the impact of increasing digital connectivity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) has been routinely overlooked2,3. This gap is particularly important for Africa, where over 60% of citizens are aged under 25 years and the population is projected to double by 20504, and for Asia, home to the majority of the world’s children and social media users2,3. While many initiatives across both regions have focused on digital inclusion to benefit children’s education5, understanding how widening internet access affects children’s exposure to online harms has become increasingly urgent.

Among the most concerning of these harms is the use of digital technologies to perpetrate sexual violence against children6,7,8, encompassing solicitation and dissemination of child sexual abuse material (images and videos), online grooming, live-streamed sexual abuse and sexual extortion8. These issues were highlighted in the 2024 US Senate Judiciary Committee9 hearing, which sought to hold popular social media companies to account for child safety issues on their platforms. Despite the efforts of multiple law enforcement authorities, UN organizations10, civil society organizations11 and national governments12, the true extent of technology-facilitated CSEA remains unclear for most LMICs, where children may face heightened risks of sexual violence13.

Effective prevention and response strategies require data-driven insights into the prevalence, root causes and effectiveness of protection systems. However, obtaining reliable data on child sexual abuse is extremely difficult. Ethical, sociocultural and safeguarding constraints limit what can be asked, how it should be asked and of whom it can be asked14. The varied international legal landscape further complicates research; in some countries legal thresholds vary and harms are not comprehensively recorded15. These challenges make research time consuming, costly and technically difficult, while limited funding and safeguarding infrastructure further constrain research capacity in LMICs16.

Here we address this evidence gap by analysing a multinational representative dataset investigating the nature and disclosure of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse experienced by children living in eastern and southern Africa and Southeast Asia. The Disrupting Harm project is a collaboration between UNICEF Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti, ECPAT International and INTERPOL, funded by the Safe Online initiative, which collected survey data from nationally representative samples of 11,912 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 years across 12 countries (Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Tanzania, Uganda, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam)17 between 2020 and 2021. These data therefore provide insights into technology-facilitated CSEA experienced by children in the African and Asian contexts.

To situate these data within current terminology, we adopt the Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (known as the Luxembourg Guidelines)18, developed through youth and expert stakeholder consultations. Importantly, this classification moves away from technological determinism while recognizing the increasingly pervasive role of technology in sexual crimes against children, across online and offline environments19. We use technology-facilitated CSEA to refer to children’s exposure to nine types of sexual harms measured in the Disrupting Harm survey (Methods). These include unwanted sexual attention through comments or images to clear instances of exploitation, including coercion into sexual conversations or activities, non-consensual sharing of children’s sexual images, offers of money or gifts in exchange for sexual content or contact and blackmail for sexual acts10. While the severity varies across these experiences, any such harms can lead to serious psychological, socioemotional and even physical consequences20. Referring to such experiences merely as risks can inadvertently contribute to the normalization of abuse21, discourage children from disclosing their experiences and even enable perpetrators to continue offending. Although not every online risk leads to harm22, adopting a harm-focused framing is crucial to fully recognizing the severity of children’s experiences, and safeguarding their rights23,24.

Research on technology-facilitated CSEA has expanded substantially in high-income countries1 yet has focused predominantly on prevalence25,26,27. Nationally representative surveys reveal wide variation in prevalence estimates due to definitional18 and methodological choices such as whether peer or adult solicitation is counted28, the recall period used (past year versus lifetime)1 and sampling denominators (all children versus internet users only)29. For example, 17.7% of Australian 16–24-year-olds reported adult online sexual solicitation before age 1830, while US estimates indicate that adding online abuse items can increase overall CSA prevalence estimates from 13.5% to 21.7% depending on how online harms are operationalized25. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis estimates that roughly 1 in 12 children globally has experienced online CSEA (pooled past-year prevalence, 8.1%)1. While such studies provide critical epidemiological functions such as mapping population burden, guiding resources, and enabling surveillance31, prevalence data alone cannot reveal whether children seek help after harm. Understanding disclosure pathways is therefore equally critical for effective prevention and response32.

To date, research on disclosure of technology-facilitated CSEA remains limited33,34. Where it exists, it often draws on forensic or criminal-justice settings35,36,37, which include victims who have already navigated formal reporting systems. Recent qualitative studies have identified barriers to disclosure such as self-blame, shame and lack of trust33, yet empirical investigations into facilitators or enablers of disclosure in online environments has been limited32,38,39,40. Evidence from broader child sexual abuse research indicates that disclosure marks a pivotal step for identifying and stopping offline sexual abuse32,41, facilitating recovery42 and reducing the long-term mental health impacts32,43,44. Children tend to first disclose to peers rather than formal reporting channels such as police, helplines or teachers32,45,46. Yet little is known about disclosure of technology-facilitated CSEA in LMICs34, where formal and informal support systems may differ substantially from those in high-income countries. Cross-cultural research on prevalence and disclosure is therefore needed to inform timely prevention, support and protection.

Guided by child-rights47 and public-health48,49,50 frameworks, we examine disclosure patterns and associated factors through a socio-ecological lens51,52,53. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child’s General Comment No. 25 affirms that protection in digital environments depends on accessible, child-friendly pathways to seek help24,47. From a public-health perspective, primary prevention (preventing abuse before it occurs) is the foundational priority, supported by secondary (early detection and intervention) and tertiary (treatment and rehabilitation) responses50. These tiers are interdependent48 as disclosure operates primarily within secondary and tertiary prevention, yet patterns of disclosure and non-disclosure can highlight how systems prevent, detect and respond to harm. When children cannot disclose, whether due to a lack of awareness, inaccessible systems or a lack of trusted adults, these barriers may signal gaps in primary prevention infrastructure50. Conversely, when disclosure does occur, timely intervention and trauma-informed care become possible. Understanding how, to whom and under what conditions children disclose technology-facilitated CSEA can therefore guide more targeted interventions, strengthen support pathways and ultimately reduce subsequent harms to children32.

In this cross-sectional study, we address two questions (Methods): (1) what are the prevalence and disclosure rates of technology-facilitated CSEA in these contexts; and (2) which demographic, family, cultural and protective factors are associated with disclosure? This study provides researchers, policymakers, child-protection and education systems and law enforcement with population-level data on children living in LMICs who are both highly vulnerable and systematically under-represented on the global scientific stage.

To address the first research question, we identify the prevalence of each of nine categories of technology-facilitated CSEA, reporting the rates for internet-using 12–17-year-old children and population-adjusted estimates for all children. Pooled across 12 nationally representative samples and surveys of 11,912 internet-using children in eastern and southern Africa and Southeast Asia, we found that one in six (17%; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 16.2–17.8; weighted n = 2,025) had experienced at least one instance of technology-facilitated CSEA in 2020–2021. Across all instances of CSEA, one in three (31%, 95% CI = 30.1–32.1; weighted n = 3,477; see Supplementary Information 2.4) internet-using children experienced some form of sexual exploitation or abuse (Supplementary Tables 3, 49 and 51), including incidents occurring online (social media, online games), in person, some other way or where the setting was not specified (do not know/prefer not to say).

Specifically, on social media or in an online game, about 10% of children received unwanted sexual images (95% CI = 9.0–10.2; n = 1,143) and 8% received sexual comments that made them feel uncomfortable (95% CI = 6.9–8.0; n = 889). Moreover, 5% (95% CI = 4.4–5.2; n = 571) were asked to discuss sex or sexual acts, while 4% (95% CI = 3.5–4.3; n = 462) were asked online to explicitly do something sexual. Furthermore, 4% (95% CI = 3.8–4.6; n = 498) of children were asked for a photo or video showing their private parts, and about 3% (95% CI = 2.4–3.1; n = 328) of children were offered money or gifts online to meet the perpetrator in person to perform sexual acts. Finally, 3% of children reported that their sexual images were shared without their consent (95% CI = 2.5–3.1; n = 332), or they were offered money or gifts to share sexual images (95% CI = 2.4–3.1; n = 324) and even blackmailed online to engage in sexual activity (95% CI = 2.1–2.8; n = 294) (Supplementary Table 50). Further details on the digital platforms and perpetrator identity associated with technology-facilitated CSEA are provided in Supplementary Figs. 17–19 and Supplementary Tables 42, 43, 47 and 48.

Country-level prevalence estimates of technology-facilitated CSEA ranged from an estimated 5.5% (95% CI = 3.7–7.3; n = 54) of internet-using children in Vietnam to 29% (95% CI = 25.3–31.9; n = 271) in the Philippines. Extended Data Fig. 1 presents survey-weighted prevalence for each specific type of technology-facilitated CSEA across 12 countries, with 95% confidence intervals. For example, less than 1% of children in Vietnam (95% CI = 0.0–1.5; n = 8) were asked to talk about sex or sexual acts online; in the Philippines, this figure was almost 9% (95% CI = 7.2–11.5; n = 89) (Fig. 1, Supplementary Figs. 2–10 and Supplementary Table 52).

To calculate the proportion of all children aged 12–17 years experiencing technology-facilitated CSEA, we multiplied each country’s internet penetration rate (collected through Disrupting Harm household surveys) by prevalence among internet users (Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2). Across 12 countries, this corresponds to approximately 10.7 million children (95% CI = 9.9 million–11.5 million; Supplementary Information 2.1–2.2 and Supplementary Fig. 15). In countries with widespread internet penetration, such as the Philippines (95%), Malaysia (94%) and Thailand (92%), the prevalence for the child population closely mirrors that among children with internet access. In countries with more limited access, such as Ethiopia (25%) and Uganda (40%), the overall prevalence among all children was 5% and 11%, respectively, reflecting differences in both internet exposure and prevalence among internet-using children. Countries with large youth populations such as Indonesia (6% among all children) and the Philippines (27% among all children) also face particular challenges as these rates translate into substantial absolute numbers of affected children. As internet connectivity continues to expand across LMICs, the population-level burden of technology-facilitated CSEA may grow substantially over the next decade.

Among internet-using children aged 12–17 years, the overall prevalence of technology-facilitated CSEA through social media or gaming platforms was nearly identical for boys and girls: 16.9% (95% CI = 15.9–18.0; n = 1,026) of boys and 17.0% (95% CI = 15.9–18.1; n = 999) of girls experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated CSEA. Prevalence increased with age from 11% (95% CI = 9.5–13.3; n = 161) among 12-year-old children to 22% (95% CI = 20.4–23.7; n = 558) among 17-year-old children (Supplementary Table 39). A Bayesian multilevel model confirmed that there is no meaningful gender difference in the probability of experiencing technology-facilitated CSEA (posterior mean = −0.01, s.d. = 0.11, 95% Bayesian credible interval (CrI) = −0.22–0.20, posterior probability of direction (PD) = 54%), with 99.7% of the posterior distribution falling within the region of practical equivalence (ROPE; odds ratios, 0.67–1.50). Older age was associated with higher probability of experiencing technology-facilitated CSEA (posterior mean = 0.18, s.d. = 0.04, 95% CrI = 0.10–0.26, PD > 99.9%), equivalent to approximately 2.7 percentage points higher probability per additional year of age (average marginal effect (AME), 95% CI = 2.2–3.1). Although the age gradient was slightly stronger for girls compared with boys (posterior mean = 0.09, s.d. = 0.04, 95% CrI = 0.01–0.17, PD = 98.5%), the overall predicted difference between girls and boys was small and the CrI included zero (AME = 0.8 percentage points; 95% CI = −0.6–2.0).

The predicted probabilities of technology-facilitated CSEA varied substantially across countries (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Fig. 21). Among girls aged 17 years, predicted probabilities were highest in Uganda (42%, 95% Crl = 0.36–0.49) and the Philippines (40%, 95% CrI = 0.34–0.47). Among boys aged 17 years, predicted probabilities were highest in Uganda (34%, 95% CrI = 0.29–0.39) and the Philippines (34%, 95% CrI = 0.27–0.40). In Vietnam, predicted probabilities were among the lowest, ranging from 3% for boys aged 12 years (95% CrI = 0.02–0.06) to 8% (95% CI = 0.05–0.11) for boys aged 17 years and 3% for girls aged 12 years (95% CrI = 0.02–0.05) to 10% (95% CrI = 0.06–0.14) for girls aged 17 years. These differences could reflect variability in the likelihood of reporting across countries rather than true prevalence differences alone.

The prevalence of technology-facilitated CSEA also varied by degree of urbanization after adjusting for gender and age (Supplementary Fig. 23 and Supplementary Table 39). Children in peri-urban settings reported the highest prevalence. Rural children had lower prevalence than peri-urban children (AME = −4.4 percentage points, 95% CrI = −7.1 to −1.9), and urban children had higher prevalence than rural children (AME = 2.4 percentage points, 95% CrI = 1.0–3.9). The difference between urban and peri-urban settings was small and uncertain (AME = −2.0 percentage points, 95% CrI = −4.8–0.7). Full model results are reported in Supplementary Tables 8 and 9.

We next identified to whom children disclosed CSEA, distinguishing between formal and informal channels. Formal channels are typically embedded within statutory child protection systems (such as police, teachers or social workers), whereas informal channels offer more personal and familial support (such as friends, family or peers). This distinction serves as an analytic heuristic to organize disclosure pathways based on the role of the recipient rather than the outcome of the disclosure (that is, whether it triggers an investigation), consistent with past research54,55 (Supplementary Table 34).

Of an estimated 2,025 children who experienced one or more forms of technology-facilitated CSEA (weighted), 51% (95% CI = 48.6–53.6; n = 1,034) did not disclose it to anyone (responses by countries and CSEA types are shown in Supplementary Fig. 24 and Supplementary Tables 40 and 41). Among those who did disclose, most did so through informal channels, including close family members, friends or other trusted adults. Specifically, 46% (95% CI = 43.1–48.1; n = 923) disclosed to friends, while many also shared their experience with family members, with 26% (95% CI = 23.6–28.0; n = 523) disclosing to siblings, 21% (95% CI = 19.3–23.4; n = 432) to mothers and 20% (95% CI = 17.9–21.9; n = 403) to fathers. Rarely did children disclose to any formal channels, such as the police (3%, 95% CI = 2.3–4.2; n = 66), helplines (3%, 95% CI = 2.4–4.2; n = 67), social workers (3%, 95% CI = 2.0–3.8; n = 59) or teachers (9%, 95% CI = 7.3–10.1; n = 177). About 6% (95% CI = 5.1–7.5; n = 127) told other trusted adults and 1% (95% CI = 0.6–1.6; n = 22) disclosed through other channels. As children could select more than one disclosure type, these percentages are non-additive (mutually exclusive categories are shown in Supplementary Fig. 25).

For non-disclosed incidents of technology-facilitated CSEA, children were asked to select all reasons why they had not told anyone. Responses were recorded per CSEA type (Supplementary Tables 45 and 46 and Supplementary Fig. 26). As respondents could select multiple barriers for each non-disclosed incident, the percentages do not sum to 100% within any CSEA type. Pooled across CSEA types (Fig. 3a), the most common barrier to disclosure was “Did not know where to go or who to tell” (37.6%, 95% CI = 35.6–39.6), followed by “feeling embarrassed, ashamed or that it would be too emotionally difficult to tell” (19.6%, 95% CI = 18.0–21.3) and “did not think it was serious enough to report” (14.2%, 95% CI = 12.9–15.7). Figure 3b shows stratified barriers by each CSEA type. For example, among non-disclosed instances of sharing sexual images without consent, 48.1% (95% CI = 39.8–56.5) cited “did not know who to tell” as a barrier, while 18.4% (95% CI = 12.8–25.9) reported feeling embarrassed or ashamed.

To address the second research question and understand the factors associated with disclosure, our analysis focused on a set of interconnected predictors across four conceptual levels: individual, family, cultural and protective. First, we examined demographic factors, such as a child’s age and gender, based on extensive evidence linking these factors to a higher likelihood of both offline and online disclosure56,57. Second, enabling parental mediation or supportive engagement by parents around a child’s use of the internet was identified as a key factor. Previous research shows that supportive parental involvement is associated with a child’s vulnerability to online risks58,59, highlighting the importance of parental scaffolding within the family unit. Third, we examine cultural factors, as well as gender norms and attitudes towards sex, including patriarchal views on violence, honour and control of girls. These factors are known to shape both the perceived severity of risks and the likelihood of disclosure in LMICs60.

Finally, we assessed a set of protective factors that may equip children with the tools and knowledge needed to report harmful experiences61, including sex education62, digital skills to report63 and children’s knowledge of where to seek help after sexual assault or harassment (help-seeking)64. Operationally, we analyse these as child-level indicators of protective factors that span the three levels of our socioecological model: acquired and enacted by children (individual), reinforced by caregivers, peers and schools (family/community), and enabled or constrained by curricula, safeguarding policies and legal frameworks (cultural).

An exploratory Bayesian multilevel model examined factors associated with children’s disclosure of technology-facilitated CSEA through any channel (that is, formal or informal). Older children were less likely to disclose these experiences (posterior mean = −0.12, s.d. = 0.05, 95% CrI = −0.22 to −0.03, PD = 99.4%) but disclosure did not differ by gender (posterior mean = 0.13, s.d. = 0.15, 95% CrI = −0.19–0.42, PD = 81.9%). By contrast, more parental involvement in children’s digital lives (that is, enabling parental mediation) was associated with higher overall disclosure (posterior mean = 0.22, s.d. = 0.08, 95% CrI = 0.06–0.38, PD = 99.4%). Similarly, children who knew where to seek help after an assault or harassment (that is, help-seeking knowledge) were more likely to disclose (posterior mean = 0.38, s.d. = 0.14, 95% CrI = 0.11–0.67, PD = 99.5%). No associations with disclosure were found for sex education, attitudes towards premarital sex, inequitable gender attitudes and digital skills to report (95% CrI crossed zero) (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 23).

Two supplementary exploratory analyses compared children’s disclosure through informal or formal channels, revealing distinct factors associated with each. Children who knew where to seek help after sexual assault or harassment (posterior mean = 0.40, s.d. = 0.13, 95% CrI = 0.15–0.66, PD = 99.8%) and who received enabling parental mediation (posterior mean = 0.19, s.d. = 0.08, 95% CrI = 0.04–0.35, PD = 98.9%) were more likely to disclose through informal channels, potentially reflecting that the former addresses a key barrier to disclosure (Fig. 3a). Children who believed in the acceptability of premarital sex (posterior mean = 0.33, s.d. = 0.16, 95% CrI = 0.02–0.64, PD = 98%) were also more likely to disclose to friends, family and other adults. Only two predictors were related to disclosure through formal channels: older children were less likely to disclose (posterior mean = −0.27, s.d. = 0.07, 95% CrI = −0.41 to −0.14, PD = 99.9%), while children who received enabling parental mediation were more likely to do so (posterior mean = 0.32, s.d. = 0.11, 95% CrI = 0.11–0.54, PD = 99.7%).

The above results reflected average trends across 12 countries, examining country-specific estimates reveals substantial between-country heterogeneity in factors associated with disclosure of technology-facilitated CSEA (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 30). For disclosure to any channel, enabling parental mediation was associated with higher disclosure in 6 out of 12 countries (95% CrI excludes 0). Knowing where to seek help was positively associated with disclosure in 4 out of 12 countries; older age was associated with lower disclosure in 5 out of 12 countries; and more inequitable gender attitudes were associated with higher disclosure in 5 out of 12 countries. Country-level estimates are further disaggregated by formal versus informal channels in Extended Data Fig. 3, underscoring the complexity of cross-cultural comparisons.
