https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Q&A: New JAMA resource shows ‘labor of love’ behind clinical trials
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades; Alison J, Huang, MD, MPhil, MAS
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

JAMA Network announced a new resource called JAMA+ Trials that is “designed to elevate the visibility, accessibility and understanding of trusted clinical trial research across medicine,” according to a press release.

The platform features a searchable collection of recent trials across the JAMA Network’s 13 journals, a rotating set of trial themes designed to stimulate conversation and debate about trials, as well as tailored educational resources on trial design, conduct and reporting.

Alison J. Huang, MD, MPhil, MAS, a clinical epidemiologist and trialist who has led multiple randomized trials and educational initiatives about trial research, will serve as JAMA+ Trials Editor in Chief, JAMA Network said.

Healio spoke with Huang to learn what gaps in knowledge the resource will address, how JAMA+ Trials could help to build public trust in clinical trials and more.

Healio: As editor in chief and a clinical trialist, what are you hoping to bring to this initiative?

Huang: I want to help the wider medical and public health community appreciate why and how trials matter. Many clinicians, patients and health system leaders have at least a superficial appreciation for clinical trials. But not that many are directly engaged in designing or carrying out a clinical trial themselves. I think many do not understand why trials are designed the way they are. Some may even have a little resentment for the burdens that come along with clinical trials. It’s understandable to ask, “Why do we have to conduct these time-consuming, costly, rigid studies? Can’t we simply troll data from health records about the effects of treatments that patients are already using, or use AI to create simulations of how new treatments could work?” So, one major goal of this initiative is to bring clarity and context to clinical trial research in a way that helps everyone who intersects with trial research to appreciate and understand it better.

Healio: What are some features of JAMA+ Trials you’re especially excited about?

Huang: There are multiple. We have launched our “Clinical Trial of the Year” series. All the editors in chief of the journals in the JAMA Network have singled out one trial from the past year that they think is especially unique, interesting or innovative, and over the year, they’re sharing their perspective on what makes those trials important or exciting in their own words. I particularly like this feature, because it illustrates the many different perspectives on what makes a trial exciting or important, from both the research and clinical side. The trials are different. Some are large, multinational trials with thousands of participants. Some are smaller trials that, despite their size, provide uniquely valuable insights. So, I think this feature showcases the diversity of trial research and all the different ways that trials can be impactful.

Then there’s our theme-of-the-month discussions, where we repeatedly explore an emerging trend, innovation or challenge in clinical trial research, seen through the lens of a rotating set of trials drawn across different disciplines. These are really turning out to be fun. We started out discussing virtual and remotely conducted trials — that is, the growing numbers of trials that are engaging participants, sometimes over widely dispersed areas, using digital platforms and tools, and trying to make it possible for people everywhere to engage in trials from their homes, workplaces and everyday lives, despite encountering challenges in realizing this vision.

Healio: Are there any general misconceptions or lack of knowledge about trial methodology that JAMA+ Trials could help bring to light and address?

Huang: Sometimes people think of clinical trial methods as being static or fixed, but trial methods are evolving. Trialists propose new statistical approaches or ways to design trials. They discuss them, they debate them, and they may disagree and criticize each other’s views. The trial field is a living, growing, adapting field. It’s part of what makes it exciting, and, hopefully, we can bring that to light. We can show the ways in which the field is changing; we can recognize differences of opinion and how trials ought to evolve.

Healio: How can the resource help to build public trust in clinical trial science and findings?

Huang: The randomized clinical trial is the one rigorous experimental study design we have in clinical medicine. It comes with a well-developed, although evolving, set of standards about rigor and transparency that are designed to protect the integrity of the research. Trialists are expected to declare their designs and methods up front, declare their endpoints in advance, and later, when they present results, show that they followed the protocol that they said they would — or if there’s a reason they had to vary from that protocol, give a powerful argument for why it was necessary. Trialists can’t simply change their methods after the fact because they don’t like the answer that the trial gave them.

The standards of blinded trials, where trial participants are masked to the interventions they’re receiving, often for years, and without any hint of what the results of the trial will be until the trial is complete, are a powerful set of conventions that are designed to resist any temptation to manipulate the results of trials.

We are in an era now where the integrity of clinical science is maybe being questioned, and JAMA+ Trials has an opportunity to showcase the aspects of trial research that are meant to protect its integrity. If there’s any form of clinical research where, as an investigator, you cannot control the outcome and you cannot force the study to tell you what you want to hear, it is clinical trial research.

Healio: What dialogue about clinical trials are you hoping to start with JAMA+ Trials?

Huang: Frankly, we just need more dialogue in general. There is surprisingly little dialogue in a field as important to medicine as clinical trials. On the one hand, we get almost all our reliable evidence about whether interventions work from trials. And yet the different sectors and members of the medical and public health community who depend on trials don’t talk that much to each other. Even among trialists themselves, there’s surprisingly little crosstalk between clinical trialists in, say, cancer vs. clinical trialists in heart disease or vs. infectious disease, or between trialists who work in the academic sector vs. those who are in industry. And then you think of everyone else who’s intersecting with trials, like regulators, payers and government entities that are deciding whether to cover and pay for health interventions, medications or procedures, and the clinicians who are also means, the consumers of trial research and are often the people making decisions.

So, members of the trial community are surprisingly siloed, and we have an opportunity to start to break down some of those silos and create more dialogue between groups and individuals who you would think would be talking actively with each other all the time but surprisingly don’t.

Part of the reason for the lack of discussion could be that sometimes the people who are most interested in trial methods may speak in arcane terms. The trial statisticians who are trying to move the field forward may speak primarily to other trial statisticians. Although on the one hand, JAMA+ Trials does want to showcase the expertise and the sophistication of those who are really steeped in trial methods, we don’t want to be an exclusive platform for niche trial methodologists to have inaccessible conversations with other niche trial methodologists. Our goal is to make trial research more intelligible to everyone who needs to conduct, support or understand it.

Healio: Is there anything else you have to add?

Huang: This platform is meant to showcase the sophistication of trial research but also the passion that goes into it. Every clinical trial is a labor of love. There is a lot of labor that goes into successively executing a high-quality trial, but it’s through that labor that we show our love for science, the evidence and the ability to change clinical practice for the better.

Alison J. Huang, MD, MPhil, MAS, a professor of medicine, urology and epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of California, San Francisco, can be reached through Hannah Alani, JAMA Network senior communications manager, at hannah.alani@jamanetwork.org.

Disclosures: Huang reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Base editing lowers PCSK9 in patients with FH, early CAD
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Genetic PCSK9 inhibition via base editing appeared safe and demonstrated dose-dependent, durable reductions in PCSK9 and LDL cholesterol, researchers reported.

At the highest dose, VERVE-102 (Verve Therapeutics) was associated with an up to 88% reduction in PCSK9 and a 62% reduction in LDL, and could represent a single-dose, lifelong therapeutic to prevent atherosclerotic CVD in people with genetic high cholesterol or premature coronary disease, according to the Heart-2 study presented at European Atherosclerosis Society Congress and simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

“For patients at high risk for cardiovascular events, such as those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia or premature coronary artery disease, clinical guidelines recommend long-term reduction of LDL cholesterol levels, potentially over a period of decades. However, the real-world incidence of discontinuation of lipid-lowering therapy across therapeutic classes, including PCSK9 inhibitors, ranges from 30% to 50% within 12 months after treatment initiation, and a lack of treatment persistence has been associated with worsened cardiovascular outcomes,” Scott B. Vafai, MD, vice president of Verve Therapeutics, and colleagues wrote in NEJM. “To overcome the limitations of the current treatment model, we developed an in vivo base editing medicine — VERVE-102 — which was designed to mimic the effects of naturally occurring cardioprotective PCSK9 variants and durably lower the LDL cholesterol level after a single infusion.”

Researchers previously presented first-in-human data from the Heart-1 trial of VERVE-101 (Verve Therapeutics), a single-dose CRISPR base-editing infusion, at the 2023 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

As Healio previously reported, VERVE-101 reduced PCSK9 and lowered LDL by up to 55% in patients with heterozygous FH and advanced CAD.

The Heart-2 trial of VERVE-102, an investigational base-editing therapy, evaluated the safety of genetic PCSK9 inhibition in 35 participants with heterozygous FH or premature CAD (mean age, 52 years; 69% men; 86% white).

Researchers reported VERVE-102 was infused for up to approximately 4 hours at one of six doses: 0.3 mg/kg, 0.45 mg/kg, 0.6 mg/kg, 0.7 mg/kg, 0.8 mg/kg or 1 mg/kg of body weight.

Participants in the present interim analysis had at least 28 days of follow-up, according to the study methods.

Seventy-one percent of participants were on a high-intensity statin at baseline while 43% were taking concomitant ezetimibe (mean PCSK9 at baseline, 455 g/L; mean LDL at baseline, 129 mg/dL), researchers reported.

All the participants received full infusions as no dose-limiting effects were observed, and only mild to moderate treatment-related reactions and brief elevations in liver alanine aminotransferase were reported.

The researchers observed reductions in PCSK9 ranging from 51% at the 0.3 mg/kg dose to 88% at the 1 mg/kg dose.

PCSK9 inhibition resulted in LDL reductions ranging from 9% at the 0.3 mg/kg dose to 62% at the 1 mg/kg dose, which corresponded to an absolute reduction of 78 mg/dL at the highest dose, according to the study.

Reductions in PCSK9 and LDL levels were durable out to 1 year in the 15 participants with long-term follow-up. Researchers noted that participants with the longest follow-up were those infused with the lowest doses of VERVE-102.

“Treatment with VERVE-102 led to dose-dependent, substantial and sustained reductions in PCSK9 and LDL cholesterol levels. Together with the safety data, these results support continued development of VERVE-102 as a treatment for hypercholesterolemia,” the researchers wrote. “Twenty years after the observation that lifelong inactivation of PCSK9 protects against atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, these data provide early clinical evidence that a single infusion of a base-editing therapy can mimic the LDL cholesterol–lowering effects of PCSK9 cardioprotective variants.”

These data are promising and build upon the field of gene editing for lipid disorders. Safety looks good, particularly compared with the first iteration of this drug. We know adherence to lipid-lowering therapy wanes over time and that is what makes a single-treatment attractive to many, particularly if LDL reductions remain more than 50% — equivalent to a high-intensity statin.

The durability of lipid-lowering response remains to be seen, but mechanistically I’d expect the effect to be permanent.

There will always be patients that will want to continue to take a daily medication or two to lower cholesterol. However, if safety signals persist for gene editing for lipid disorders, many people will likely opt for a one-time therapy if given the option. Illustrating this is the large number of patients that reached out to us at C5Research after we published the data for gene editing of ANGPTL3 in November, asking to be considered for future trials when they take place in the U.S.

Vafai SB, et al. Late breaker abstracts in PCSK9 pharmacology. Presented at: European Atherosclerosis Society Congress; May 24-27, 2026; Athens, Greece.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Weight loss did not impact persistent AF burden
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

A low-calorie diet and behavioral support program conferred weight loss in older participants with obesity and persistent atrial fibrillation but did not significantly improve AF symptoms vs. usual care, researchers reported.

The observed weight loss also did not appear to significantly reduce physical performance testing or need for repeat cardioversion or AF ablation in the patient population, according to data published in JAMA.

“The dietary weight-loss and behavioral support intervention was quite effective in inducing weight loss, almost 10% of body weight,” Rohan Wijesurendra, MB, BChir, MA (Cantab), MSc, DPhil (Oxon), FRCP, FESC, honorary consultant cardiologist and electrophysiologist at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, told Healio. “However, despite this successful weight reduction, we did not see a clinically important improvement in AF symptoms, AF burden, cardiac remodeling or subsequent rhythm-control procedures over the study period.”

For the prospective, open-label LOSE-AF trial, researchers randomly assigned 118 participants aged 60 to 85 years with persistent AF and BMI of 27 kg/m2 or more referred for direct current cardioversion to either an 8-month low-calorie diet and behavioral support intervention or usual care (mean age, 68 years; 33% women).

Participants assigned to the intervention group were referred to a structured dietary weight-loss and behavioral support program and assigned a counselor who provided behavioral coaching, weight monitoring and formula meal products, according to the study methods.

Researchers reported the control arm received usual care with a single face-to-face consultation with a research nurse and educational materials on dietary weight loss.

At baseline and 8 months, researchers evaluated AF symptoms using the Atrial Fibrillation Severity Scale, anthropometric measures, clinical history, ECG, Physical Performance Test, EuroQoL 5-Dimension 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) health status, cardiac MRI and lipid profile as well as 14-day ECG patch monitoring (BodyGuardian MINI, Boston Scientific) at follow-up.

“The issue of AF and obesity comes up frequently in my clinical practice,” Wijesurendra told Healio. “Weight loss is encouraged in AF guidelines as part of comprehensive risk-factor management, but randomized data supporting this approach are sparse generally, and particularly limited in older patients with established persistent AF. That evidence gap was a major motivation for conducting LOSE-AF.”

Participants assigned to the low-calorie diet and behavioral support intervention experienced a 9.7% weight reduction compared with a 3.1% weight reduction in the usual care arm (P < .001) and no serious adverse safety events, according to the study.

The researchers reported no significant difference in Atrial Fibrillation Severity Scale score (between-group difference, 0.9; 95% CI, 3.3 to 1.4; P = .43) or any other outcome of interest including Physical Performance Test and incidence of repeat cardioversion or AF ablation during follow-up.

“The lack of clear AF-specific benefit was notable, although perhaps not entirely surprising,” Wijesurendra told Healio. “Many participants had longstanding persistent AF, and in older patients this is often associated with more advanced atrial remodeling. This may make it harder to modify the arrhythmia with weight loss alone, at least over the short to medium term.

“Clinically, these data should not discourage weight management, which remains important for overall CV and metabolic health,” Wijesurendra said. “However, our results suggest that dietary weight loss alone may be insufficient to achieve rhythm control in older patients with persistent or longstanding persistent AF. Additional treatments, such as antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation, may be needed for patients in whom rhythm control is an important treatment goal.”

Rohan Wijesurendra, MB, BChir, MA (Cantab), MSc, DPhil (Oxon), FRCP, FESC, senior clinical research fellow, University of Oxford, honorary consultant cardiologist and electrophysiologist at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and stipendiary lecturer in clinical medicine at St John’s College, University of Oxford, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Sclafani M, et al. JAMA. 2026;doi:10.1001/jama.2026.5787.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: ‘Excitement and interest’ as Lp(a) therapies inch closer
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Editor’s Note: This is part two of a two-part Healio Exclusive series on Lp(a). Part one can be seen here.

Late-phase trials of targeted therapies for elevated lipoprotein(a) are nearing completion, with the first readouts expected later this year.

“All the progress in the last 20 to 30 years has now led to targeted therapies for Lp(a) and that’s what’s driving a lot of the excitement and interest right now. There are finally therapies that are hopefully very close to being available,” Harpreet S. Bhatia, MD, MAS, FACC, FAHA, FASPC, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine, associate program director of cardiovascular diseases fellowship and director of exploration and innovation at the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine, told Healio.

Dedicated therapies are in varying stages of clinical development and address elevated Lp(a) through several mechanistic paths, including injectable antisense oligonucleotides, oral small molecule inhibitors, injectable small interfering RNA therapies and gene editing.

“From a risk reduction standpoint, these novel therapeutics may ultimately all perform similarly, but we’ll need outcomes data to know for sure. Another important aspect that we’re going to have to be paying attention to is the safety profile of the different agents,” Michael C. Honigberg, MD, MPP, cardiologist and researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital and assistant professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, told Healio.

There are no therapies currently approved to lower Lp(a). The new American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends initiation of lipid-lowering therapy and risk factor management for people with and Lp(a) level of 125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) or more.

“In order to treat Lp(a) effectively, we have to interrupt the assembly of the Lp(a) particles — that is, the assembly of the apolipoprotein A-I component to the [apolipoprotein B] component,” Healio | Cardiology Today Editorial Board Member Steven E. Nissen, MD, MACC, chief academic officer of the Sydell and Arnold Miller Family Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute and the Lewis and Patricia Dickey Chair in Cardiovascular Medicine at Cleveland Clinic, said in an interview. “One way to do that is to interfere with messenger RNA for ApoA. ApoA is the rate-limiting step, and if you don’t make ApoA, you don’t make Lp(a).”

Pelacarsen (Ionis/Novartis) is a monthly, self-injected antisense oligonucleotide therapy designed to lower Lp(a). It is being evaluated for secondary prevention in the ongoing phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial, which enrolled about 8,300 patients with a prior atherosclerotic CVD event and Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL.

“The first drug to really show big effects is pelacarsen,” Nissen told Healio. “[Ionis/Novartis] worked with my team and I to develop a trial initiated around 2020 called Lp(a)HORIZON. We have announced that it will be read out in the second half of this year.”

Phase 2 data published in The New England Journal of Medicine showed that pelacarsen 20 mg weekly reduced Lp(a) by approximately 80% over 16 to 17 weeks compared with placebo.

As Healio previously reported, pelacarsen is also being evaluated in the Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS trial, which will evaluate the effect of Lp(a) lowering on progression of calcified aortic stenosis.

“Pelacarsen will be likely the first drug to complete its trial and, assuming it’s positive, will likely be the first drug to come to market for Lp(a) lowering,” Bhatia told Healio.

Several injectable small interfering RNA therapies are currently in development for Lp(a) lowering, including lepodisiran (Eli Lilly), olpasiran (Amgen) and zerlasiran (Silence Therapeutics).

“They’re all in various stages of development. But the zerlasiran and olpasiran trials are well along. These drugs are double-stranded RNA, and they have a more persistent effect than pelacarsen,” Nissen told Healio.

As Healio previously reported, both lepodisiran and olpasiran are dosed less frequently —every 6 months and 12 weeks, respectively — than pelacarsen and have been shown to durably reduce Lp(a) by up to 95%.

Zerlasiran was evaluated in the phase 2 ALPACAR. Researchers reported zerlasiran lowered Lp(a) by at least 90% at 36 weeks and reduced LDL up to 31.9%, according to results published in JAMA.

Oral therapies for Lp(a) lowering are also in development, including muvalaplin (Eli Lilly), HRS-5346 (Merck/Jiangsu Hengrui) and YS2302018 (AstraZeneca/CSPC Pharmaceutical Group). These therapies are in earlier phases compared with pelacarsen and the injectable small interfering RNA therapies.

As Healio previously reported, muvalaplin was the first oral therapy developed to target Lp(a). In a phase 2 study, muvalaplin reduced Lp(s) levels up to 80% in patients with Lp(a) of 175 nmol/L or more and a history of coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease, familial hypercholesterolemia or type 2 diabetes.

Muvalaplin is currently being evaluated in the phase 3 MOVE-Lp(a) trial.

HRS-5346 is currently being evaluated in a phase 2 trial in China at three separate doses in patients with elevated Lp(a) and prior ASCVD and/or high risk for ASCVD, according to a company press release. YS2302018 is in preclinical development and will be evaluated alone and combined with an oral PCSK9 inhibitor (enlicitide, Merck), according to a company press release.

Although not directed at Lp(a) reduction, nonstatin lipid lowering via cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibition may have off-target effects that reduce ASCVD risk in this population, according to a presentation by Bhatia at the 2025 American Society for Preventive Cardiology Congress on CVD Prevention.

Obicetrapib (NewAmsterdam Pharma) is being developed alone and with ezetimibe as a treatment for LDL lowering. A pooled analysis of the ROSE1 and ROSE2 phase 2 trials showed that the CETP inhibitor lowered Lp(a) by more than 57% compared with placebo.

“Obicetrapib does seem to have an effect, but it’s not been thoroughly tested and the evidence is not as robust. Trials are underway,” Nissen told Healio.

Recent data published in NEJM have shown the potential for gene-editing therapy (CTX310, CRISPR Therapeutics) to lower atherogenic lipids in patients with uncontrolled hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia or mixed dyslipidemia despite maximally tolerated lipid-lowering therapy. CTX310 is designed to induce permanent ANGPTL3 gene loss of function and is intended to be a one-time treatment for high LDL and triglycerides.

Another research-stage gene-editing therapy (VERVE-301, Verve/Eli Lilly) is currently being developed to permanently deactivate the LPA gene. This therapy incorporates a novel in vivo gene editing mechanism that lowers Lp(a) by permanently deactivating the Lp(a) gene in the liver according to a company press release.

“If you’ve got a drug you can give twice a year, that is attractive. How much more attractive it will be to knock out the gene remains to be seen,” Nissen told Healio. “But we’ve certainly got a long way to go before these products are actually ready for prime time.”

One treatment will not “win out” over the others, Bhatia said, since some of the current therapeutics being evaluated will initially have more evidence for the secondary prevention population while ongoing trials of other therapies will provide evidence for the primary prevention population.

“Even though these therapies are not yet available, they are close. In the meantime, there are still things that we do every day to help manage individuals with high Lp(a),” Bhatia said. “Now is a great time to get tested.”

Healio wants to hear from you:

Until a targeted therapeutic is approved, how are you managing atherosclerotic risk in patients with elevated Lp(a)? Share your thoughts with Healio by emailing the author at sbuzby@healio.com or tagging @CardiologyToday on X. We will contact you if we wish to publish any part of your story.

Harpreet S. Bhatia, MD, MAS, FACC, FAHA, FASPC, can be reached at hsbhatia@health.ucsd.edu.

Michael Honigberg, MD, MPP, can be reached at mhonigberg@mgh.harvard.edu or X @mchonig.

Steven E. Nissen, MD, MACC, can be reached at nissens@ccf.org.

Disclosures: Bhatia reports consulting and/or advising for Amgen, Merck and Novartis. Honigberg reports serving as a site investigator for the Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS trial for Novartis and a trial of lepodisiran for Eli Lilly. Nissen reports serving as study chair for the HORIZON trial sponsored by Novartis, for which he does not receive personal financial compensation.

https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.title: No added MACE risk associated with biologics, immunomodulators
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.author: Octavia Feliciano
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The risk for major adverse cardiovascular events appeared similar between older patients treated with 5-aminosalicylic acid and those who received immunomodulators or biologics for inflammatory bowel disease, data show.

“Our findings are reassuring in that immunomodulators and biologics were not associated with elevated cardiovascular risk,” Tianze Jiao, PhD, assistant professor in the department of pharmaceutical outcomes and policy at the University of Florida, told Healio.

“This [research] supports consideration of these therapies when clinically indicated, without substantial concern for excess cardiovascular harm,” Jiao added.

Chronic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction associated with IBD may drive the increased risk for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), according to prior research.

Researchers noted that use of advanced therapies to control inflammation associated with IBD could consequently reduce risk for MACE. However, published data were mixed, with one study linking biologics to a higher risk for MACE when compared with placebo.

In the study, Jiao and colleagues were interested in clarifying whether different IBD therapies impact cardiovascular risk among older adults with IBD. They conducted a comparative effectiveness study using a random sample of 16,387 Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries (mean age, 74.73 years; 60.18% women) first prescribed immunomodulators, biologics or 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) for IBD between 2012 and 2020.

Patients were followed for up to 3 years or until their prescription was switched or discontinued.

Time to first ED or inpatient visit due to MACE, which included myocardial infarction, stroke or all-cause mortality, served as the study’s primary outcome.

After propensity matching to balance patient demographics, comorbidities and medication use, two cohorts were created: one comparing immunomodulators with 5-ASA (n = 4,384) and one comparing biologics with 5-ASA (n = 3,064).

Risk for MACE did not significantly differ between 5-ASA and biologics (HR = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.59-1.24) or immunomodulators (HR = 0.84; 95%CI, 0.61-1.17).

“Consistent with prior pharmacologic and pathophysiologic evidence, our study suggested that advanced therapies, especially biologics, may potentially reduce cardiovascular disease risk compared with 5-ASA through systemic anti-inflammatory effects,” Jiao said.

“Although these associations did not reach statistical significance, likely because of limited sample size and event rates, the direction and magnitude of the estimates were clinically intriguing,” he said.

Limitations of the study include the short median follow-up time, only 6 to 10 months, and lack of data on patients’ IBD activity indices, inflammatory markers and BMI.

“Accounting for these factors in future studies could help clarify the mechanisms through which anti-inflammatory therapies influence cardiovascular health,” Jiao said.

Longitudinal studies drawing on data from electronic health records could explore this pathway, according to Jiao.

“Clinicians should continue to individualize anti-inflammatory treatment decisions based on disease severity, including with use of biomarkers, patient characteristics and preference,” he said. “Importantly, our findings suggest that advanced therapies may even confer potential cardiovascular benefits through systemic inflammation reduction, although additional studies are needed to confirm this hypothesis.”

Tianze Jiao, PhD, can be reached at tianzejiao@ufl.edu.

Jian Q, et al. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9091

Disclosures: Jiao reports no relevant financial disclosures. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.title: Stroke risk greater in older adults with migraine with aura
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.author: Kristen Dowd
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Migraine with aura was associated with an increased risk for incident ischemic stroke in middle-aged adults, with no difference among Black and white patients, according to a study published in Neurology Open Access.

Lead study author Adam S. Sprouse Blum, MD, PhD, clinical instructor at the Larner College of Medicine at the University of Vermont, and colleagues further found that any migraine with or without aura was linked to a greater risk for ischemic stroke in men aged younger than 72 years, which was not found in women or older men. The study authors called this finding “contrary to expectations.”

“Previous research has shown that migraine with aura is linked to an increased risk of stroke in younger people but less is known about people 45 years old and older,” Sprouse Blum said in a press release related to the study. “Our study found that similar to younger people, migraine with aura was associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke in middle-aged and older adults.”

Sprouse Blum and colleagues culled data from the REasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in Stroke cohort to include 11,381 adults aged at least 45 years (mean age, 72.1 years; 55.2% women; 34.8% Black) in their study. At baseline, participants had not yet had a stroke and were asked about migraine incidence.

During a mean follow-up of 6.4 years, 44 of the 1,130 participants (3.9%) who experienced migraine also experienced ischemic stroke; of the 10,251 participants without migraine, 351 (3.4%) experienced the same. Further, of the 491 adults who reported migraine with aura, 23 (4.7%) reported ischemic stroke. Fewer individuals with migraine without aura (21 of 639; 3.3%) reported the same.

The authors reported the incidence of stroke, calculated per 1,000 person-years, to be 6 in those with migraine — including 7.2 for migraine with aura and 5.1 for migraine without aura — and 5.4 in those without migraine.

The overall risk for ischemic stroke in adults with migraine was not significant in fully adjusted models (HR = 1.35; 95% CI, 0.98-1.87), Sprouse Blum and colleagues wrote. While no association for ischemic stroke was found for those with migraine without aura, the study showed a 73% increased risk among adults who experienced migraine with aura (HR = 1.73; 95% CI, 1.12-2.65).

After stratifying by sex and age, the researchers discovered men aged younger than 72 years with migraine had a 3.5 times increased risk for ischemic stroke (HR = 3.67; 95% CI, 1.96-6.88), regardless of whether they had aura. This finding was not seen in women or in men aged 72 years and older.

The study did not uncover any migraine-by-race interaction.

“Our result that middle-aged and older male participants under age 72 had a much higher risk of stroke was unexpected since previous research in young people has shown that stroke disproportionately affects female individuals,” Sprouse Blum said in the press release.

Future studies are needed to further understand and confirm these findings, he added.

“Should the findings be confirmed, it may be necessary to provide targeted stroke prevention counseling for individuals in this age group,” Sprouse Blum said.

The finding that migraine with aura, but not migraine without aura, was associated with an independent increased risk of incident ischemic stroke is not surprising, as it has been reported in several prior studies as described in the study’s discussion section.

However, the finding that the highest migraine-associated risk of ischemic stroke was in males younger than the age of 72 years was surprising to me for two reasons: One, a significant association of migraine and ischemic stroke was not found in women; and two, in the male group aged younger than 72 years, the migraine-stroke association was significant in both those with aura and without aura.

As a stroke and migraine specialist, most of the patients I have seen with migraine-related stroke have been young and middle-aged women. I have, however, also diagnosed older middle-aged men with migraine-related stroke, my husband being one of them. Mostly these individuals had active history of migraine with aura and the work-up often suggested cardio embolism. But anecdotal experience needs to take a back seat to the findings in this study, which has notable strengths: prospective design, large sample size, high-risk age group, inclusion of Black and white individuals and strong adjudication of stroke.

I agree with the authors’ suggestion in the concluding paragraph that there may be an increased need to screen for migraine and provide counseling in male adults in order to prevent stroke.

Since the finding that the highest risk of ischemic stroke was in adult males (age < 72 years) with migraine (both with and without aura) is novel, it is important that it be confirmed through further research in similar populations.

Sprouse Blum AS, et al. Neurol Open Access. 2026;doi:10.1212/WN9.0000000000000107.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Heart-healthy habits may have prevented cases of severe COVID-19
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Measures of ideal heart health including healthy levels of physical activity, BMI, BP and sleep were associated with lower risk for severe COVID-19 among people with no history of heart disease during the pandemic, researchers reported.

For every 1 standard deviation increase in total American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score, individuals without prior CVD experienced an approximately 20% reduced risk for severe COVID-19 infection, according to data published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

“What's well known in COVID epidemiology research at this point is that persons with CVD suffered greater consequences from COVID than those without, and during the ‘heyday’ of the pandemic, we identified early on that people with heart disease were at a much higher risk for consequences from the disease, such as death and hospitalization. This begs the question, what about people without CVD? How does overall heart health relate to risk for COVID-19?” Timothy B. Plante, MD, MHS, associate professor of medicine at Larner College of Medicine at the University of Vermont, told Healio. “What seems to be a repeating theme is that heart health predicts pretty much every outcome under the sun, not just heart disease and stroke.

“There’s a clear gradient between CV health and risk for bad outcomes, the bad outcome here being severe COVID-19. It’s yet another demonstration that CV health is not just important for heart health, but spans all sorts of different health events, including COVID-19,” Plante said.

Heart health in the present study was measured using the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 tool, with the following metrics: diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep, body weight, lipids, blood glucose and BP. Each component of Life’s Essential 8 was scored on a scale of 0 to 100 then averaged to determine an individual’s total score. A score of less than 50 was defined as poor CV health, a score of 50 to 80 as moderate CV health and a score of higher than 80 as high CV health.

Researchers evaluated the impact of heart health on COVID-19 severity using the nationwide, prospective C4R study, which includes aggregated data from 14 NIH-funded studies. Participants were recruited as long ago as 1971, and the present study included all living participants not lost to follow-up as of March 1, 2020, according to the study methods.

Data on clinical and subclinical diseases, risk factors and social determinants of health were gathered during follow-up, and questionnaires, events surveillance and serosurveys were used to identify those with COVID-19 infection during the pandemic from March 2020 to February 2023.

After excluding participants with CVD at baseline or during follow-up, the present cohort consisted of 29,740 individuals (mean age, 66 years; 61% women; 35% white; 22% Black; 34% Hispanic), of whom 681 experienced severe COVID-19.

Researchers reported that higher Life’s Essential 8 score was significantly associated with lower risk for severe COVID-19 infection (adjusted HR per 1 standard deviation increase = 0.8; 95% CI, 0.73-0.88). One standard deviation in the present study was defined as 14 points on the Life’s Essential 8 scale, Plante said.

Compared with participants with poor CV health, those with high CV health had lower risk for severe COVID-19 infection (aHR = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.37-0.78) but risk did not vary between those with poor CV health and those with moderate CV health (aHR = 0.81; 95% CI, 0.64-1.04), according to the study.

Researchers noted the relationship between higher Life’s Essential 8 score and lower risk for severe COVID-19 infection remained consistent regardless of age, sex, race/ethnicity, educational attainment or vaccination status.
The Life’s Essential 8 components most strongly associated with lower risk for severe COVID-19 were high scores in physical activity, BMI, BP and sleep, according to the study.

“Our paper demonstrates there’s perhaps some ways we could identify folks most likely to benefit from harm prevention strategies during a viral pandemic, whether it be COVID, the next SARS viremia or something else, using something as simple as CV health. The other implication is that it helps explain why there were so many deaths from COVID-19 in the U.S. Overall CV health levels in the U.S. are not particularly great. Perhaps had we had better CV health among the U.S. population, we may have experienced fewer hospitalizations or deaths,” Plante told Healio. “There’s just yet another reason to encourage people to do the right things for their heart, whether that be exercise, quit smoking, sleep better, get BP under control and so on.”

Timothy B. Plante, MD, MHS, associate professor of medicine and physician scientist at Larner College of Medicine at the University of Vermont, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Plante TB, et al. J Am Heart Assoc. 2026;doi:10.1161/JAHA.125.048256.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Lp(a) and cardiovascular risk: What you should know
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Editor’s Note: This is part one of a two-part Healio Exclusive series on Lp(a). Part two can be seen here.

A single lipoprotein(a) screening in a person’s lifetime could significantly reduce their risk for heart disease-related morbidity and mortality, yet this opportunity is often missed.

Screening for elevated Lp(a) and targeting modifiable risk factors and lifestyle could meaningfully lower risk for atherosclerotic CVD and potentially thrombosis, even in people with very high levels.

No targeted therapies are currently approved to lower Lp(a) levels, but that does not mean nothing can be done to mitigate its impact on cardiometabolic health.

Lp(a) is an atherogenic, prothrombotic particle distinct from LDL in that it carries a single apolipoprotein(a) strand bound to its ApoB-100 component, according to the recently updated American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia, published in Circulation and Journal of the American College of Cardiology in March.

“Lp(a) is important because it is more strongly associated with cardiovascular morbidity and mortality than many traditional lipids such as LDL cholesterol,” Healio | Cardiology Today Editorial Board Member Steven E. Nissen, MD, MACC, chief academic officer of the Sydell and Arnold Miller Family Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute and the Lewis and Patricia Dickey Chair in Cardiovascular Medicine at Cleveland Clinic, said in an interview. “For a long time, it didn’t receive much attention. Elevated Lp(a) is common. Depending on what cut point you use, about one in every five individuals has an Lp(a) level in a range where there is increased risk. That’s more than 1 billion people on our planet, and it has taken a while for the guidelines to recognize it.”

What makes Lp(a) different from other lipid particles is that levels are mostly determined by genetics, with more than 90% of measurable circulating levels linked to a single gene, making it a potent, inheritable ASCVD risk factor, according to Harpreet S. Bhatia, MD, MAS, FACC, FAHA, FASPC, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine, associate program director of cardiovascular diseases fellowship and director of exploration and innovation at the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine.

Nissen said if a patient has elevated Lp(a), the concordance among first-degree relatives is approximately 47% that they also have high Lp(a).

“Earlier studies failed to show an association between Lp(a) and CVD. One of the reasons for that is that Lp(a) is hard to measure. It’s a complex particle, and prior studies used ways of measuring Lp(a) that were less accurate,” Bhatia told Healio. “The field was revived when genome sequencing-type studies became easier and cheaper, and it was clear that the LPA gene was strongly associated with CVD.”

In the updated guideline, one-time Lp(a) screening for all adults was made a class I recommendation to identify individuals at increased risk for ASCVD.

“We have definitely seen an increase in testing as awareness has spread about Lp(a) being a significant cardiovascular risk-enhancing factor. However, testing in the general population is still less than 1%, so we still have work to do,” Allison Bigeh, DO, noninvasive cardiologist at Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, told Healio. “Currently the recommendation is to test once in everyone. The reason being Lp(a) is genetically determined, so it is not influenced by things like lifestyle changes or diet. There are certain conditions like pregnancy that can affect the levels, but for the most part Lp(a) levels are established very early in life before adolescence.”

Discussion of risk stratification continues.

In 2024, the National Lipid Association (NLA) issued a focused update, published in the Journal of Clinical Lipidology, on Lp(a) in clinical practice with recommendations for risk-stratification based on Lp(a) levels. According to the NLA statement, high risk was defined as Lp(a) of 125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) or more, intermediate risk was defined Lp(a) of 75 nmol/L to 125 nmol/L (30 mg/dL to 50 mg/dL) and low risk was defined as Lp(a) levels less than 75 nmol/L (30 mg/dL).

In the American Heart Association/ACC guideline, Lp(a) was established as a significant ASCVD risk factor at levels exceeding 125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL).

“Some people would argue that risk starts to go up as soon as you get above the upper limit of normal, which is 75 nmol/L,” Nissen told Healio. “But risk is graded and it goes up as you get to higher levels of Lp(a).”

Long-term studies with serial Lp(a) testing have shown that both high and low levels remain unchanged over time, Bhatia said.

“It’s that intermediate-risk group where 40% to 50% of people might move between the risk categories,” Bhatia told Healio. “Those are individuals in whom repeat testing could be helpful, particularly if a new condition develops that could affect Lp(a) levels, like menopause, hypothyroidism or chronic kidney disease.”

Michael C. Honigberg, MD, MPP, cardiologist and researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital and assistant professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, said repeated testing may be reasonable in specific situations, but current data do not clearly support rescreening.

“The guidelines endorse using this threshold of 125 nmol/L, but we actually know risk is linear and continues to rise with progressively higher Lp(a). There is nothing magical about 125 nmol/L other than it represents roughly the top 20% of the population distribution,” Honigberg said. “Many Lp(a) clinical trials of novel therapeutics are enrolling patients with an Lp(a) level of 175 nmol/L or higher, which the NLA calls ‘very elevated Lp(a),’ and we know from other data that levels around 300 nmol/L confer roughly equivalent risk as familial hypercholesterolemia. That’s a class I recommendation for lipid-lowering therapy. Based on those data, I treat modifiable risk factors, including LDL, very aggressively in individuals with those more extreme levels of Lp(a), similar to how I would approach familial hypercholesterolemia.”

An Lp(a) level of 125 nmol/L or more is associated with an approximately 1.4-fold increased risk for ASCVD, and Lp(a) of 250 nmol/L or more is associated with more than twofold higher risk, according to the American Heart Association/ACC guideline.

The guideline authors stated that levels of 125 nmol/L or more warrant intensified lipid-lowering therapy and management of all possible modifiable risk factors to prevent ASCVD events.

“Intensively treat every other risk factor. Get LDL and BP down. Treat diabetes and obesity. We can mitigate at least some of the risk by taking care of all the other risk factors,” Nissen said. “We can’t treat the Lp(a), but we can treat everything else, and that’s an important component of why we think it ought to be measured in everybody.”

Aspirin 81 mg daily may reduce CV events in patients with elevated Lp(a), but no prospective trials have been done to date, Bigeh told Healio.

Bhatia said aspirin may play a direct role in reducing the “theorized prothrombotic and particularly proplatelet effects of Lp(a).”

For patients with established ASCVD and elevated Lp(a) who are not at target LDL and non-HDL goals despite maximally tolerated statin therapy, the addition of a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended in the American Heart Association/ACC and NLA guidelines. However, statins may slightly increase Lp(a), according to the both documents.

In the U.S., lipoprotein apheresis (Liposorber LA-15 System, Kaneka) is FDA approved with an indication for Lp(a) lowering in high-risk patients with FH and ASCVD and is the only currently available therapy directed to specifically lower Lp(a).

“The prior attitude was if Lp(a) is genetically determined, and people can’t do anything about it, what is the point of screening?” Honigberg told Healio. “Lp(a) is not destiny, but it makes comprehensive risk factor management a lot more important.”

Eventually, clinicians may have options beyond risk factor management for patients with elevated Lp(a). A number of drugs specifically targeting Lp(a) are in development, and the first phase 3 trial results are anticipated later this year.

Editor’s Note: Part two of this Healio Exclusive series will delve into the pipeline of Lp(a) therapeutics.

Healio wants to hear from you:

How are you screening for Lp(a)? Share your thoughts with Healio by emailing the author at sbuzby@healio.com or tagging @CardiologyToday on X. We will contact you if we wish to publish any part of your story.

Harpreet S. Bhatia, MD, MAS, FACC, FAHA, FASPC, can be reached at hsbhatia@health.ucsd.edu.

Allison Bigeh, DO, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Michael Honigberg, MD, MPP, can be reached at mhonigberg@mgh.harvard.edu or X @mchonig.

Steven E. Nissen, MD, MACC, can be reached at nissens@ccf.org.

Honigberg reports serving as a site investigator for the Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS trial for Novartis and a trial of lepodisiran for Eli Lilly. Nissen reports serving as study chair for the HORIZON trial sponsored by Novartis, for which he does not receive personal financial compensation.

https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.title: Prednisolone fails to reduce arterial lesions in Kawasaki disease
https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.author: Jason Laday
https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Adding prednisolone to standard therapy for Kawasaki disease failed to prevent coronary artery lesions 1 month following disease onset, according to data published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

“The current standard primary treatment for Kawasaki disease is high-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) with aspirin,” Siyuan Lin, MD, of the Children’s Hospital of Fudan University and National Children’s Medical Center, in Shanghai, and colleagues wrote. “However, coronary-artery lesions develop in approximately 10% to 20% of treated patients, and 8% to 25% have resistance to IVIG, which is a known risk factor for coronary-artery lesions. This situation underscores a need to improve primary treatment to reduce coronary-artery lesions.

“The effect of adjunctive glucocorticoids in the primary treatment of Kawasaki disease remains controversial,” they added. “Current guidelines recommend adjunctive glucocorticoids for patients at high risk for resistance to IVIG. However, critical gaps in research remain.”

To examine the impact of adjunctive glucocorticoids on the incidence of coronary artery lesions in Kawasaki disease, Lin and colleagues performed a multicenter, open-label, randomized, controlled trial of 3,208 newly diagnosed patients in China. The researchers assigned the patients 1:1 to receive either prednisolone plus standard treatment or standard treatment alone.

Prednisolone was administered in dosages of 2 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, for a maximum dose of 60 mg. Standard therapy involved IVIG administered at 2 g per kilogram, for a maximum dose of 60 g, and oral aspirin at 30 mg per kilogram per day divided into three doses. Aspirin doses were lowered to 3 mg to 5 mg per kilogram per day, maintained for at least 6 weeks, after fever had resolved for 3 days and CRP levels were deemed normal, the researchers wrote.

Incidence of coronary-artery lesions at 1 month after disease onset served as the primary outcome. Key secondary outcomes included the use of rescue therapy, duration of fever, change in the C-reactive protein level, and changes in coronary-artery z scores. Analyses for key secondary outcomes were not controlled for multiplicity.

According to the researchers, 16% of patients who received prednisolone alongside standard treatment demonstrated coronary artery lesions, vs. 13.8% for those who received standard therapy alone (adjusted risk difference = 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, –1 to 3.4).

In all, 4.6% of patients in the prednisolone group received rescue therapy vs. 10.1% of those who received standard therapy alone. Reductions in coronary-artery z scores were similar between both groups. The incidences of coronary-artery lesions at 3 months were 12.6% in the prednisolone group and 10.5% among those who received standard therapy.

The percentages of patients with coronary artery lesion progression were 28.6% for the prednisolone group and 28.9% for standard therapy alone, with incidences of medium-to-giant coronary-artery aneurysms reported at 1.9% and 1.1%, respectively. According to the researchers, the incidences of adverse events were similar between both groups.

“In our trial, the administration of glucocorticoids in addition to standard primary treatment did not reduce the incidence of coronary-artery lesions at 1 month among Chinese children with Kawasaki disease,” Lin and colleagues wrote. “Future studies are needed to better assess longer treatment and follow-up duration of glucocorticoids or other immunomodulating therapies to reduce the burden of coronary artery disease in patients with Kawasaki disease.”

Lin S, et al. N Engl J Med. 2026;doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2511478.

Disclosures: This study was funded by the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. Lin reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.title: HHS rolls back changes to rules for membership on CDC vaccine panel
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.author: Sara Kellner
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

A rewritten charter for the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee that would have loosened the rules for membership to allow for less qualified members has been withdrawn.

A document published in the Federal Register on May 19 states that the renewal for the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices charter was withdrawn due to “an administrative error in meeting the revised public notification timing requirements under the revised Federal Advisory Committee Act regulations, as amended in December 2025. As a result, the charter lapsed and the committee must be re-established.”

The previous charter for the influential panel, which guides federal vaccine policy, said ACIP members should have knowledge or expertise in the field of public health, vaccines or vaccine research. HHS revised the language in April to expand the qualifications for membership to include expertise in toxicology, pediatric neurodevelopment, data science, statistical analysis, health economics and recovery from serious vaccine injuries. That revision came less than a month after a federal judge revoked the appointment of most voting members based on their lack of experience in relevant fields.

The judge also temporarily blocked an overhaul of the CDC’s childhood immunization schedule that was published in January, pending an appeal by the Trump administration.

Reuters reported that HHS withdrew the revised charter following criticism that the new language would allow health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to reappoint the committee members who were blocked by the judge’s order. A new charter signed by Kennedy on May 14 no longer includes toxicology or data science as required areas of expertise, according to Reuters. Healio has requested a copy of the new charter.

“My main concern is returning to evidence as the basis for vaccine policy in the U.S.A.,” Kevin A. Ault, MD, FACOG, FIDSA, an ACIP member from 2018 to 2022, told Healio. “I am not sure that this version of the charter will take us in that direction.”

Ault said he is not sure what this change means for the ACIP at this time.

“Right now, we don’t have a functional way to make vaccine policy without a CDC director,” Ault said.

The CDC has been functioning without a permanent director since last August, and for most of President Trump’s second term. Trump’s nomination last month of former deputy surgeon general Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, to lead the CDC was received with enthusiasm by experts.

A date for Schwartz’s hearing with the Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pension committee has not been publicly announced. The committee is in charge of vetting nominations for CDC director before they are moved to the Senate for a full confirmation vote.

NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, MD, PhD, is currently performing the duties of CDC director.

Kevin A. Ault, MD, FACOG, FIDSA, is a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Western Michigan University and vice president of the board for the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases. He can be reached at pediatrics@healio.com.

Disclosures: Ault reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/amazon-fo.title: Jeff Bezos’ 25-year-old stress cure is to ‘make the first phone call, or send the first email’—and a recruiter says it lands even harder in 2026
https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/amazon-fo.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/amazon-fo.text:
With economic uncertainty, AI anxiety, and a brutal job market weighing on workers everywhere, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has a counterintuitive theory on coping with stress—and thinks most people get it completely wrong.

Back in 2001, the then-new tech billionaire, fresh off Amazon’s 1997 IPO, took to the stage at the Academy of Achievement Summit in San Antonio to lay out a take on what actually causes stress. And in his eyes, it has nothing to do with workload, grueling hours, or needing a holiday.

“You can be working incredibly hard and loving it,” Bezos said. “And likewise, you can be out of work and incredibly stressed.”

The culprit, Bezos argued, isn’t your workload. It’s inaction.

“People get stress wrong all the time, in my opinion,” he added. “Stress comes from ignoring things that you shouldn’t be ignoring.”

The fix, Bezos says, is simple—and it doesn’t require even solving the dilemma that’s making you lose sleep. You just need to do something, anything, to chip away at it.

“Stress primarily comes from not taking action over something that you can have some control over, so if I find that some particular thing is causing me to have stress, that’s a warning flag for me,” Bezos explains. “What it means is there’s something that I haven’t completely identified, perhaps in my conscious mind, that is bothering me, and I haven’t yet taken any action on it.”

“As soon as I identify it and make the first phone call, or send off the first email—whatever it is that we’re going to do to start to address that situation—even if it’s not solved, the mere fact that we’re addressing it dramatically reduces any stress that might come from it,” he added.

In other words, the relief doesn’t come from resolution. It comes from motion.

And he made his point with a concrete (and eerily prescient) example: two people can both be out of work, but the one grinding through job applications and interviews will feel far less stressed than the one sitting at home spiraling. Same situation. Completely different headspace.

“If you’re out of work, but you’re going through a disciplined approach—a series of job interviews and working to remedy that situation—you’re going to be a lot less stressed than if you’re just worrying about it and doing nothing,” Bezos said.

Fortune contacted Bezos for comment.

The Amazon and Blue Origin founder’s advice feels more relevant now than ever, as young people stare down an uncertain economy, a wave of AI-driven redundancies, and the worst job market we’ve seen in 37 years.

“Bezos is right, and I think it lands even harder in 2026 than it did when he first said it,” Lewis Maleh tells Fortune. As CEO of the executive recruitment agency Bentley Lewis, he sees it play out constantly. “Most of the stress I see in candidates isn’t about uncertainty or workload. It’s about the gap between what they know they should be doing and what they’re actually doing. Inaction is the real tax.”

For the millions of unemployed young people—or NEETs—Maleh shares some tangible steps they can take to regain some sense of control.

“If you’re waiting to hear back after an interview, the worst thing you can do is sit with your phone,” he says. “Reconnect with five people in your network who already know your work. Write something publicly that puts your thinking into the world. Take a course. Pick up a freelance project. Most of the relief comes from the action itself, because action restores agency, and agency is what kills stress.”

If you’ve got a job, but you’re feeling stuck and stressed as a result, Maleh says “apply less, network more.”

“Most senior hires are made long before a role is ever posted,” he explains, adding its why instead of shooting out hundreds (or even thousands) of applications into the job ad abyss, workers can take charge by deciding who they want to work with and “work backwards from there.” Pluck up that conversation with an old colleague, train up for the next role you want, and post all about it.

“Make yourself easy to refer,” he adds. “Become the obvious answer to a question people are already asking.”

Ultimately, whether you’re pining for a new job, promotion, or change of direction in your career, the responsibility for making it happen sits with you. And as Bezos put it 25 years ago, taking ownership for your own success is a lot less stressful than waiting for someone else to fix it—and even less stressful than doing nothing at all.

“Be the CEO of your career,” he adds. “No one else is going to run it for you. Not your employer, not the market, not a recruiter, and certainly not LinkedIn’s algorithm. The moment people stop outsourcing responsibility for their own trajectory is usually the moment the stress starts to lift.”
https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/amazon-fo.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says most people get stress wrong all the time. He says it's not your workload, but it's inaction. He suggests a disciplined approach to dealing with stress can reduce stress.

https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/us-soccer.title: U.S. Soccer is using AI to scout 70 million teenagers. The former consulting CEO running the federation calls it a ‘paradigm shift’ for the sport
https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/us-soccer.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/06/02/us-soccer.text:
For 30 years, American soccer has been the sport of the almost. Almost breaking through. Almost finding its footing. Almost fielding the team its passionate, fast-growing fan base deserves. The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup, kicking off this summer across American stadiums, was supposed to be the moment of arrival—but the federation responsible for putting the best possible team on the field has been quietly grappling with a structural problem that no amount of cultural momentum could fix on its own.

It has never been able to reliably find its own best players.

Now, Dan Helfrich—who retired last year as CEO of Deloitte Consulting to take on what he calls a “passion project” running the U.S. Soccer Federation as its chief operating officer—says AI is about to change that in ways the sport has never seen. “My view is we can actually scout every single soccer match that a U.S.-eligible player is playing anywhere in the world,” Helmbridge said at the Fortune COO Summit in Scottsdale, Ariz. “Think about that paradigm shift.”

The scale of the challenge is unlike anything in American sports. Because U.S. Soccer eligibility flows through citizenship and parentage—not birthplace—American-eligible players are scattered across every continent, suiting up in leagues from Lagos to Leipzig to Lima. Helfrich puts the number at between 50 million and 70 million teenagers, boys and girls, playing on any given day.

The federation’s human scouting network was never built for that. “How do you get your scouts—your humans—to all of those places?” Helmbridge said. “You can’t. And so automatically, you’re excluding 99.5% of people.”

That is not a rounding error. It is a structural ceiling that has persisted for as long as the American game has existed—and it compounds with every passing generation of players who were simply never seen. Add in the “pay-to-play” youth club system that has long screened out talented kids from lower-income families before any scout arrived, and the blind spot becomes a chasm. The American soccer machine has been operating, for decades, with most of its inputs switched off.

Helfrich said two things are now “converging” simultaneously: the explosion of video availability for youth sports globally, and the rapid maturation of AI-powered video analysis tools. Together, they make something that was previously unthinkable suddenly achievable.

The system works by training AI models on positional profiles—defining the specific movement patterns, spatial awareness, and technical markers U.S. Soccer looks for at each position—and then deploying that analysis at scale across video feeds regardless of where in the world they originate. A right winger running channels for a youth club in Boise gets the same level of algorithmic attention as one playing for a powerhouse academy in New York or a semi-professional feeder side in Germany. For the first time, geography stops being a disqualifier.

“We have this extraordinary challenge operationally to find all the American-eligible teenagers around the world who are playing at any given day,” Helfrich said. “Video becoming much more widely available for youth sports, and AI—suddenly, we’re reimagining.”

Helfrich was careful not to declare the human scout obsolete. The AI handles volume and geography—the things no person can do alone—but there are dimensions of elite evaluation it cannot yet replicate. “What’s the tone of voice of a player to a teammate when the teammate makes a mistake?” he said. “Really hard thing to detect. What’s the body language when the team goes up or goes down?”

The model that emerges is explicitly hybrid: AI surfaces candidates at a scale previously impossible, and human scouts assess the intangibles that cameras can’t decode. It is the same restructuring playing out across industries from finance to medicine—not replacement, but a force multiplier that expands what the human expert can actually see and act on. For a former Deloitte Consulting CEO who spent decades deploying that logic in professional services, the soccer application is, he admits, considerably more enjoyable. “In my old job, I had a lot of examples that weren’t as fun,” Helfrich said. “This one is a fun one to relate to.”

The urgency is real. Soccer has spent three decades becoming something in America—slowly, organically, against the grain of every prediction that said it would happen faster. Roger Bennett, cofounder and CEO of Men in Blazers and one of the sport’s most astute observers, delivered the headline-making verdict earlier this year when he appeared on Alex Rodriguez’s podcast: Soccer has already overtaken baseball as America’s third-most popular sport, according to Q4 2024 research from Ampere Analysis cited by The Economist. Five billion people will watch the World Cup this summer. NBC Sports’ opening weekend of the 2025-26 Premier League season was the most-watched on record in the U.S.

The fan base, in other words, is enormous and growing. The commercial infrastructure is in place. What has lagged is the on-field product—and Bennett, who has watched the USMNT’s results with the particular anguish of a true believer, is unsparing about why. “When we play a big team, we still have an inferiority complex,” he told Fortune recently. “An imposter syndrome.” The U.S. has won exactly one knockout-round game in World Cup history. A so-called golden generation of players has been producing a diet of largely meaningless friendlies.

That gap—between America’s booming soccer culture and its underperforming national team—is exactly what makes the AI scouting bet so consequential. The talent may always have been there, dispersed across 70 million eligible teenagers on six continents. The federation simply lacked the tools to find it.

“Be realistic, do the impossible,” Helfrich said, borrowing the federation’s own mantra. For a sport that has spent 30 years being told its moment was coming, an AI-powered talent revolution—built quietly, in the background, while the World Cup spotlight blazes—may be the most structurally important thing American soccer has ever done.

Win or lose this summer, the search is on—this time, with robots.

https://fortune.com/2026/06/01/grey-rhin.title: Grey rhinos, black swans, and the kidnapping of Nancy Guthrie: What Corporate America still gets wrong about risk
https://fortune.com/2026/06/01/grey-rhin.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/06/01/grey-rhin.text:
When Savannah Guthrie’s 84-year-old mother was abducted in Arizona earlier this year, the FBI issued an unusual warning: in the age of AI, even a proof-of-life video can’t be trusted. A kidnapper now needs little more than a LinkedIn photo and a voicemail to manufacture a convincing deepfake. The old rules of crisis response no longer apply.

It was, said Sid Kosaraju, president of global security firm Crisis24, exactly the kind of threat corporations have been slow to take seriously. A hush came over the room at the Fortune COO Summit in Scottsdale as Kosaraju described the actual threat landscape that most people would rather not think about.

Two years into his role, he said, he asked his own security team to run a cyber assessment. He considered himself well-protected. But his team — ethical hackers — were able to pinpoint the location of his 12-year-old daughter in two-hour increments, every day, simply by accessing her school’s website and her tennis club’s schedule. She doesn’t even own a smartphone. “They could get into the school website. They could get into the tennis club website and pinpoint.”

Usually what happens, Kosaraju explained, is that threat actors target children and elderly parents. “Sorry to say here right in this state of Arizona, we have the Guthrie incident.” These are things that the industry is wrestling with right now, he said. “It’s not just the principal. It’s the families that you have to protect against.”

The Nancy Guthrie case was, he added, what the industry calls a “grey rhino” — a massive, visible, charging threat that most of us have been staring at for years and chose not to act on. The phrase, popularized by Michelle Wucker in the 2016 book of the same name, was intended to challenge decision makers to confront these challenges, instead of “willfully ignoring them and getting trampled,” Wucker told Fortune. It’s not a “black swan,” the term popularized by Nassim Taleb for unknowable, unpredictable catastrophes. A grey rhino: obvious in retrospect, ignored in the moment.

That distinction, argued Kosaraju and Kroll CEO Jacob Silverman, in conversation with Fortune‘s Ruth Umoh, is the single most important concept in risk management that corporate America is still getting wrong.

Most executives think about security as something that happens at the perimeter — a firewall, a badge reader, a background check. Silverman, who leads one of the world’s foremost corporate investigations and risk advisory firms, calls that a category error.

“The weakest link is always a person,” he said. “And some of the biggest threats — purposeful or inadvertent — come from within the walls of all of our organizations.”

That’s the grey rhino: not a sophisticated nation-state attack, but a routine online calendar, visible to anyone who looks.

Silverman was blunt about what AI has done to the threat landscape: it has made deception cheap, fast, and nearly undetectable. His firm, Kroll, fields impersonation attempts constantly — fake emails, fake invoices, fake voices purporting to be him.

“I can’t tell you how many times Jake Silverman asked for billing information,” he said, by way of example. “And now with the ability to do real deepfakes with AI, it’s all that much more dangerous.”

The FBI’s warning in the Guthrie case crystallized what security professionals have been saying for years: the proof-of-life paradigm — the foundational mechanism of kidnap response for decades — is broken. AI needs only seconds of audio or a single photograph to generate a convincing fake. Verifying that a loved one is alive, in real time, has become a genuine technical and operational challenge.

The corporate implications run wider than kidnapping. When your employees, your customers, and your fellow executives can no longer assume that an email, a voice call, or a video is real, the entire architecture of organizational trust requires rethinking.

At the Fortune 100 level, Kosaraju described an intelligence infrastructure that would have seemed excessive even five years ago: dedicated business resiliency teams staffed with former CIA and FBI analysts, feeding real-time geopolitical intelligence to C-suite executives on a continuous basis. Some executives now receive what amounts to a daily presidential brief — a document summarizing threats to their people, facilities, vendors, and supply chains, generated and synthesized by AI.

Silverman’s firm, Kroll, is operationalizing a similar capability. Its Resolver platform uses AI to ingest security information and help risk managers run remediations with an audit trail, cutting the lag time between detecting a breach and containing it.

But here’s what struck the audience: the median annual security spend on C-suite protection at the top 100 publicly listed U.S. companies was under $100,000 as recently as 2023. That figure, Kosaraju noted, has risen sharply in the two years since — but the baseline was startlingly low for organizations with global exposure.

For companies without Fortune 100 budgets, both executives converged on three affordable, underutilized baselines:

Training, both stressed, underlies all of it. Kosaraju’s firm uses a rotating verbal password system: if an employee receives a suspicious communication claiming to be from a senior executive, they call a designated number and exchange a code.

Silverman closed the conversation with the frame that should unsettle every COO in the room. Threats today don’t arrive in silos.

“When something is a physical threat, it usually is linked to a supply chain threat, which is linked to a business threat and linked to a cyber threat,” he said. “They all come together at you at one time.”
